questions.stem: A trivia tournament organizer wanted to study the relationship between the number of points a team scores in a trivia round and the number of hours that a team practices each week. For the study, the organizer selected 55 teams at random from all trivia teams in a certain tournament. The table displays the information for the 40 teams in the sample that practiced for at least 3 hours per week. Number of points per round Hours practiced 6 to 13 points 14 or more points Total 3 to 5 hours 6 4 10 More than 5 hours 4 26 30 Total 10 30 40 Which of the following is the largest population to which the results of the study can be generalized?

options.A: All trivia teams in the tournament that scored 14 or more points in the round
options.B: The 55 trivia teams in the sample
options.C: The 40 trivia teams in the sample that practiced for at least 3 hours per week
options.D: All trivia teams in the tournament

questions.stem: A market researcher selected 200 people at random from a group of people who indicated that they liked a certain book. The 200 people were shown a movie based on the book and then asked whether they liked or disliked the movie. Of those surveyed, 95% said they disliked the movie. Which of the following inferences can appropriately be drawn from this survey result?

options.A: At least 95% of people who go see movies will dislike this movie.
options.B: At least 95% of people who read books will dislike this movie.
options.C: Most people who dislike this book will like this movie.
options.D: Most people who like this book will dislike this movie.

questions.stem: A survey was conducted using a sample of history professors selected at random from the California State Universities. The professors surveyed were asked to name the publishers of their current texts. What is the largest population to which the results of the survey can be generalized?

options.A: All professors in the United States
options.B: All history professors in the United States
options.C: All history professors at all California State Universities
options.D: All professors at all California State Universities

questions.stem: A school estimates student satisfaction by surveying 30 students who attend the optional celebration. What is the main concern?

options.A: Random assignment bias
options.B: Selection bias, because attendees may be more satisfied than other students
options.C: The sample is too representative
options.D: The survey necessarily proves causation

questions.explanation: B is correct. The sampling location systematically favors a subgroup likely to differ in satisfaction.

questions.stem: In a study of 35 neighborhoods, areas with more bike lanes also have newer buildings and lower traffic noise. The study attributes the outcome entirely to bike lanes. What is a key concern?

options.A: The study used too many measurements.
options.B: Bike lanes cannot be associated with the outcome.
options.C: Related neighborhood differences may be confounding variables.
options.D: A correlation automatically rules out confounding.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Other neighborhood characteristics related to both the explanatory feature and the outcome can confound the association.

questions.stem: A survey of 40 members of one garden club finds that most prefer native plants. The report concludes that all homeowners share that preference. What is wrong with the conclusion?

options.A: It uses a sample rather than a census, which is always invalid.
options.B: It reports a preference rather than a numerical value.
options.C: It fails to impose a treatment even though the goal is only to describe a preference.
options.D: It overgeneralizes from a narrow, unrepresentative sample.

questions.explanation: D is correct. A narrow convenience group is not a representative basis for a much broader population claim.
